In my opinion, this is an utterly ridiculous ruling. I know that it's standard,
but it's ridiculous. If you can only play stealth/intercept if you need it, then
you shouldn't be able to play a +2 stealth action if your prey/predator don't
have any minions with permanent intercept bonuses. In fact, if your predator and
prey have no minions, you shouldn't even be able to play +1 stealth actions.
Since you can obviously play such an action, you should be able to use the Second
Tradition. Second Tradition is a reaction that allows a tapped vampire to block
an action. This block just happens to be at +2 intercept, just as Movement of
the Slowed Body happens to be at +2 stealth. Explain to me how the two are
different.

(Note: I am not contesting the "only if needed" rule. You shouldn't be able to
play Precognition or Faceless Night or whatever if stealth/intercept is not
needed. I contend that Second Tradition (just like +N stealth actions) is a
special case. Just as the particular action must play the card to be attempted,
Second Tradition must be played for a block to be possible. The
stealth/intercept are additional affects. )

-Chris

You need to check the rules more thoroughly.

The stealth and intercept dumping rules work like this. A vampire
cannot play a stealth modifier unless the vampire attempting to block
has and equal or greater amount of intercept. However, he can play any
source of stealth at any level (within the limits of his abilities, card
text etc.) A similar situation exists with intercept, except for the
fact that the stealth has to be greater than your intercept before you
can play an intercept card. However, you can use any source of
intercept at any level (again, card texts and abilities permitting).
And, of course, in all circumstances, pay attention to any errata etc.

So, let's just take a silly example.

Agripina declares a bleed against you, using Computer Hacking. Now, if
it had been one bleed, you might have been tempted to let her through,
but being as its two, you decide to have an attempt to block her.
Perusing your hoard of minions, you find the only untapped vampire you
have with any Auspex is Aleph. A quick appraisal of your hand shows you
that you only an Enhanced Senses to hand, which might come in useful if
Agrippina puts up any resistance - you weren't expecting to use much
intercept, but the little bit you have has come in handy.

Aleph attempts to throw up a little bit of resistance at The Incognito
Swiss Bank, to prevent Agrippina wiping out your assets there, declaring
a block. Agrippina, though, has a few tricks up her sleeve. Since your
intercept (0) matches her stealth (0) she can play a stealth card at any
level. Her hand has been a bit jammed recently, so she only has one
stealth card to hand - a copy of Swallowed by the Night. She throws
that down, cloaking the whereabouts of her link from Aleph's view.

Aleph grins happily. He knew that training in being a human radar would
help :) Summoning up all of his concentration, he throws down an
Enhanced Senses. Since he's got less intercept than you have stealth,
you can play any source of intercept until you have a greater or equal
amount of intercept. Aleph expects Agrippina to have a few more tricks
up her sleeve, so he screws up all his ability into one burst, managing
to use Enhanced Senses at superior, for +2 intercept.

Agrippina, though, thinks that she will have to show this little upstart
just what a master of deception she can be. Luckily, as a replacement
for her Swallowed by the Night, she was fortunate enough to pick up a
Cloak the Gathering. Well, she can only play it at inferior (and none
of her fellow minions have it at superior anyway), so she throws that
down. She knows it might be futile, she might have exhausted her powers
of deception but it gets another trick out of her way so that she can
progress further and further into far more devious and manipulative
things.

So, the score currently stands at Agrippina wih +2 stealth, and Aleph
with +2 intercept. Aleph can't play any more intercept, since Agrippina
has to play some more stealth before he can. Anyway, you didn't pick up
another intercept card from your replace anyway.

Agrippina's controller goes to replace his Cloak the Gathering. His
eyes light up! A Lost in Crowds...... Agrippina picks up her laptop
and flees. Aleph still has her in his sights and starts to close on
her. He didn't bank on Agrippina managing to lose him, though, by
slipping into the hoards of people demonstrating in the streets. Evades
him she does, and evades him completely... gone beyond all hope of
finding her...... well, there goes any chance of a couple of weeks
someone nice, dark, dank and cold this year... Aleph consoles himself,
though, comfortable in the knowledge that Agrippina won't be able to
keep up that standard of ability for long.... or so he hopes.

Since the Lost in Crowds is, again, only one source of stealth,
Agrippina can throw it down at either level. Working on the principle
that she *needs* to get this bleed done, she doesn't want any surprises
from you drawing another intercept card. So, as in many, many cases,
she decides to throw it down at superior (I suppose that if you had
thrown down excess intercept (eg You'd gone to +2, I only had +1 and
only had a Lost in Crowds in hand) I might have chosen to throw it down
at only the inferior level if I wanted to get into combat with you).

So, the final tally stands at +4 stealth, +2 intercept, with Agrippina
running off happily into the night, pleased with a job well done.

Now, where do I apply for that Noble Prize for Literature then? :)

The whole reason I think there's such a hullabaloo about Second Tradition
(as opposed to other kinds of "intercept dumping") is that the prohibition
against 2nd Trad. makes the vamp unable to block at all (barring other
card play). This is unique. In other kinds of intercept dumping the
action is already blocked. Since the whole purpose of intercept is to be
able to block, to be unable to block _because_ you're gaining intercept
turns the whole concept on its head.

I don't dispute that the way the current "intercept dumping" rule is stated
prevents a vampire from using 2nd Trad. to block an action for which the
vamp doesn't need 2nd Trad's intercept. Nonetheless, I think people would
find it more natural if the intercept-dumping rule were instead:

"You may not gain unneeded intercept, unless the minion would otherwise
be unable to block the action unassisted."

Perhaps the wording would need further tweaking, but I think this rule
would allow 2nd Trad. against actions where intercept is not needed,
without allowing other kinds of intercept dumping.

And of course the current rulings on 2nd Tradition make the card incredibly
weak. Except possibly for 6th Tradition, it is now the weakest of the
traditions. I don't think the card was designed to be this weak. To use
2nd Tradition, you have to make sure to tap your princes, leave someone
else untapped to block actions (or include wakes) to force opponents to
stealth actions, make sure your untapped minions don't get Misdirected,
rushed or tapped blocking early actions, make sure both your princes and
other untapped minions are capable of handling combat from blocks -- _then_
you can use 2nd Tradition.

I really hate explaining how 2nd Tradition "really works" to non-Net-aware
Methuselahs...because it's wonky!

Your post containing the "my point is this" includes four points:

> b) A minion who cannot block does not need intercept.

a) is correct (explicit rules).
d) is correct (card text).

b) is properly stated as "a minion only needs intercept when he is
attempting to block a minion whose stealth is greater than his
intercept".

Since a minion who cannot block will obviously not be attempting
to block, your statement is true, but not germaine to the Second
Tradition argument.

c) is not true.

A Prince who "cannot block" the current action (because of Blood
Bond or Incriminating Videotape or whatever) cannot use Second
Tradition.

You are trying to use "cannot block" to mean "is tapped". Being
tapped implies "cannot block" only as much as not having
enough intercept implies "cannot block". If either is true,
then you cannot block, but a minion in either of these
situations can block by untapping or gaining sufficient intercept,
as appropriate. So they "can block" the current action in the
strict sense (unlike the Blood Bond or Incriminating Videotape
cases, where the minion really "cannot block").

Your argument would mean that a minion cannot ever block an action
that has more stealth than he has inherent intercept, since

"A minion who cannot block" (by your usage) includes not only
tapped minions but also minions who don't have enough intercept to
block.

and

"b) A minion who cannot block does not need intercept."

In sum (to repeat):
1) Playing Second Tradition will untap you and make you attempt to
block with +2 intercept. (This is the sum, complete, instantaneous
effect of playing Second Tradition - the effect does not resolve
in stages).
2) Since the card will make you block and add intercept, you cannot
play it unless you need intercept for that block.

No, I think you're wrong. 2nd Tradition is a blocking card with the side
effect of granting +2 intercept. There is no prohibition against gaining
intercept as an integral part of declaring a block; the prohibition only
kicks in after a block is declared. To rule otherwise requires errata.
Consider LSJ's rules outline:

E. An attempt to block is resolved as follows: (18.2) [13.3]
1. Pick (untapped) blocking Minion. (18.2.1)
2. Stealth and Intercept. [13.3.2]
a. Blocking Minion can play a Reaction card to increase Intercept only
if the Acting Minion has Stealth greater than the Blocking Minion's
Intercept. (:18.2.3) Any cost of the the Reaction is paid.
b. Acting Minion can play an Action Modifier card to increase Stealth
only if the Blocking Minion has at least as much Intercept as the
Acting Minion's Stealth. (:18.2.2) Increased stealth lasts until the
action is finished. [13.3.2]
c. Repeat a,b above until neither Minion wishes to play a card.

All intercept cards I can think of besides 2nd Trad. have to be played in
step 2a. 2nd Tradition _cannot_ be played in step 2a because 2a occurs
after a block declaration, and 2nd Tradition declares a block. 2nd
Tradition must be played in step 1, to pick a blocking minion. There is
no prohibition against gaining intercept in step 1; to rule so requires
errata. Referring back to the original VTES rules book, there is no
explicit prohibition against gaining intercept as a block is declared;
the prohibition is again only after block declaration.

> > Section 17 Stealth and Intercept
> > You may not increase a minion's stealth unless another minion is
> > attempting to block, and you need to overcome that minion's intercept.
> > Similarly, you may not increase a minion's intercept unless it is trying to
> > block a minion whose stealth is higher.
>

My website. Rules -> VTES Rulebook.

> As is, it
> would seem to prohibit Psychic Projection and Mr. Winthrop.

Possibly. If so, those "break the rules" by implicit meaning (like
Rampage), since you can never need intercept at the time those
are adding intercept.

> "10) You may play cards and abilities that provide stealth only if any
> minions have attempted to block the current action, but not if the acting
> minion's stealth exceeds all of those minions' intercept. You may play
> cards and abilities that provide intercept only if the minion you want to
> play them on has attempted to block the current action, but not if your
> minion's intercept exceeds the acting minion's stealth."
>

> Is the above "full text" what gets approved by the RT, or is this text
> just a paraphrase of a decision?

Unknown - so "Full Text" would be the obvious assumption.

> If it's not a paraphrase, it has some

> problems. It seems to prohibit Psychic Projection and Mr. Winthrop.

> Assuming that this inadvertent prohibition is just an oversight of some
> kind, let's ignore it for now.
>

> The above text would also either seem to prohibit 2nd Tradition outright,
> or allow it in all cases, depending on how you read the second sentence.
> Since intercept can only be played by a minion that "has attempted to

> block", which is past tense, it would seem to be impossible to play
> intercept simultaneously with block declaration. Alternatively, since

> 2nd Tradition is clearly played at block declaration, and the second

> sentence doesn't cover cards played at that time (or before that time,
> e.g. Psychic Projection), the prohibition against gaining intercept doesn't
> apply to 2nd Tradition.

Right. So, by the RTR text, you can only add intercept if you have
previously attempted, even if you are not currently attempting, to
block (the current action).

One can imagine that this is not correct, and instead should have
said "A minion may only use cards and abilities that provide
intercept only when attempting to block an acting minion whose
stealth exceeds this minion's current intercept."

I'll send it back to the RT for correction.

Incidentally, it also incorrectly treats all previous would-be
blockers as current blockers. For instance:

Aggripinna bleeds.
Maskia blocks.
Aggripina plays Cloak for +1 stealth.
Masika plays Enhanced Senses for +2 intercept.
Aggripina plays Elder Impersonation to render Masika incapable of blocking.
Rake attempts to block.

At this point, Aggripina can dump stealth (say, Lost in Crowds), since
Masika's intercept is sufficient to allow her to do so.

If she does so, by the RT text, Masika can play Spirit's Touch (since
he "has attempted to block" and Ag's stealth exceeds his intercept),
even though he can't actually block.

Again, the RT text is short-sighted. I'd recommend playing it the
right way, since RT replies are widely spaced in time.

Ok, let me first point out that I see where everyone is coming
from who wants to be able to use 2nd Tradition on a 0 stealth
action.

We can all agree that 2nd Tradition is an intercept card, correct?
The intercept it gives is simultaneous with the untapping and blocking
effect. As such, it cannot be used as a means to untap and block
a 0 stealth action.

So why not change it to what some feel is more intuitive (ie makes
sense in a game world sense)? Well, let's look at what else that
would open up:

Intercept - If you can use one intercept card when you don't need it,
why not the others? Then an intercept deck can just dump intercept
on a block until it gets the combat cards it wants. After all, why
does the acting minion have to be really sneaky for the blocking
minion to have hightened senses and to read auras?
Net Effect - The game loses some of the deck design
intracacies as balancing intercept and combat cards isn't
_as_ important as it was.

Stealth - If the blockers can dump cards, why not the acting guy, too?
Afterall, why does the blocker have to be just barely sneaky enough
to get passed the blocker? As someone else pointed out, why does
someone have to try to find me before I can make myself be lost in a
crowd?
Net Effect - Same as dumping intercept. In a S&B deck, you
don't have to balance your bleed modifiers and your stealth
modifiers as much. And not blocking a S&B deck is one way
to slow it down.

Weapons - Why can't I use a Brass Knuckles while under the effects of
an Immortal Grapple? Or Sengir Dagger? Or Bang Nakh? Is a Bastard
Sword too big? What about a Saturday Night Special or a .44? All
these could be intuitively interpreted to be usable under an IG.

The list could go on. Once you change one card to be intuitive to
fit with what would make sense in a real World of Darkness, you open
a whole new ball of wax. If people want to play their game that
way, that's great...for their group. But we have to have a standard
for all of us to play in.

I find it somewhat annoying that when I play with a new group, I have
to learn all their house rules, too. I'd much rather be able to just
refer to LSJ's references for any problems. Perhaps this bit is more
suited for a different thread, so I'll stop there.

Just some thoughts,

>lots of effort and verbiage was spent on trying to find some justification in
>the rules to make the card work the way we want it to. Sadly, it simply is not
>there. I agree that the card would make more sense if it worked in some way
>that allowed it to be used when you don't need the intercept. However, there
>is a vast difference between trying to change the rules to fit the card (which
>is pretty much what one entire side of this debate is trying to do) and
>changing the card to fit the rules (which is a completely different thread to
>the current one.)

I do not believe that's true. Of course, I may not have read the whole
thread closely enough. But what I have read seem to argue for a change
in the rules themselves which would have the effect of fixing this problem
with this card - and possibly others.

>"I'm not sure what point you're trying to make. Like or lump it? "
>
>I think my point is pretty clear. The rules say the card works in a certain
>way. If you don't like the way the card works, you are much better off trying
>to change the card, not the rules. Changing the _rules_ to fit a card is
>incredibly inconsistient and makes the game into more of a mess. Changing the
>_card_ is a fairly common wish.

I disagree. Sometimes changing a rule can make a single card or a whole
class of cards work "better" (in a given person's opinion, of course). If
so, it may well be easier to change the rules than to errata the card.
Errata bad. Specific, contrived card-rulings bad. Rule changes better.

>"Sorry - distinction noted. None the less, the rules don't have to "work like
>this"."
>
>But yes, they do. Changing the rules in an inconsistient way makes the game a
>huge mess.

Er, who's talking about "changing the rules in an inconsistent way"? We're
just talking about "changing the rules", period. I'm not sure what you're
afraid would become inconsistent. You could certainly change the rules in a
consistent way and cause this change...depending on what you mean by
"consistent". If you mean, "consistent with how it was played in the past",
probably not. But who cares?

>If you change them for 2nd Trad., why not change them for Bonding,
>and then Spirits Touch, and then Brass Knuckles, and then Deflection...

Well, why not? It's a question of opinion. One would have to propose the
specific rule change before I could state mine.

>If the rules were changed to say "You cannot play a card that increases your
>intercept, unless you need it, _or_ if the card makes more sense that way..."
>you open a really big and ugly door to loopholes and addenda.

I agree. So _that_ particular rule change probably wouldn't be a good one.
But your imagination is very limited if you that's the only way a rule
change could be phrased to make 2nd Tradition more intuitive. Why not,
"You cannot play a card that ONLY increases your intercept, unless you need
it." Just by adding the word "only", I've proposed a self-consistent, easy-
to-understand modification to the rules which solves the problem folks are
discussing in this thread. You may find some flaw in it or not like the
effect it has on other cards but consistency is not a problem (or at least,
point out how the change causes a consistency problem; I don't see one right
off). And if you don't like that one, there's probably a zillion other ways
you could change the rules that would bypass your objections. It's just a
matter of employing sufficient cleverness in proposing the change. And
in the end, it's opinion whether or not the game would play better or not
given a well-considered proposal.

Fred

Because (as I've stated repeatedly) the rule itself is rather counter-

>> But you still don't

>

>What's wrong with that? Why should there be something wrong with a card

I addressed that in the text you cut out of my previous post:

# I'm not saying games should never have such cards. Sometimes (for instance),
# it's necessary for CCGs to print cards like that to play-balance other
# aspects of the game or sometimes because weird can be good for shaking up
# play and keeping the players on their toes - sort of like how the otherwise
# lowly Spy in Stratego works. If you like such things. But you still don't
# tend to expect cards to reward lack of stealth when stealth is otherwise
# treated as completely good for all other purposes.

To further elaborate, if your game is full of such tricks and traps -
advantages that suddenly become disadvantages, trick cards that reverse
the field and make the bad good and stuff like that - then people can plan
to play the game with that in mind and it can be kind of funky. I don't
really see V:tES being that sort of a game, though. Do you? Ultimately,
though, this boils down to a question of taste. I agree that it's a
mistake to overly villify the way ST is officially ruled to work. I just
don't think the proposal to change the rules and make it work differently
should be villified, either. Debated, certainly. Disputed, perhaps. But
not villified.

>> >If the answer is "no", then it seems like you should be able to accept 2nd
>> >Tradition as just a kooky card which works in a weird way.

>> work in (this particular) weird way." It's certainly a reasonable opinion.
>

>If everyone got to change every card to the way they wanted it, this
>game would be unplayable.

It depends on what you mean by this. You mean, should we dole out the
card ruling assignments to separate work-at-home-netreps and let them
each rule as they please without worrying about overall consistency? That's
silly, of course. But if you mean, you can't change the overall rules to
have the effect of changing the way a single card works, sure you can. You
may feel it's too much trouble to go to to tinker with the general rules
just fix one single card but you can certainly do it in a reasonable manner
which would not make the game the _least_ bit unplayable if you really wanted
to.

Mind you, I'm not saying you can really twist a rule one way then the other
to produce separate effects for generally like cards because you would simply
rather that some cards worked one way and some otherwise identical cards
worked a different way. But no one's proposed anything like that. The
problem people see with ST can almost certainly fixed with a fairly simple,
reasonable rule change.

>> >As I have said from the beginning, I totally understand why people would
>> >like the card to work differently, but that I feel that this desire
>> >should not be the only reason to make it so.
>>
>> And why not? Justify that.
>

>Because you want the card to work differently. I don't want the card to
>work differently. Who wins? I think the best answer is "the rules
>win".

Er, you mean the _existing_ rules win. Essentially status quo rules uber
alle? Sure, if there's really a division in how people feel, let well
enough alone may well be the best means of deciding the issue. (Assuming
WotC even cares what we thing about it.) But by itself, its clearly not a
reason to argue against changing a rule. First of all, explain _why_ some
significant number of people are against change. Just because, "I always
did it that way and my daddy always did it that way and my grampy always
did it that way and, hell, Hamblins been doin' it that way since the Civil
War!!!"? Sounds mighty conservative to me.

>If everyone plays the cards the way they want to instead of the
>way the rules say the cards work (to as great an extent as possible),
>then two people from different groups can't even play the same game.

I agree. So this can be done two ways: either folks stop complaining about
the existing rule and just lump it or the rule changes and everybody starts
doing it the other way. Either one works.

>> Of course,
>> folks can always play "house rules" if it bothers them too much but if
>> large numbers of people like it better changed, why make the universal
>> rules reflect this so people can construct decks to play against strangers
>> and in tournaments with this in mind?
>

>Because when someone who isn't on the net comes to a tournament, they
>will expect the game to be played the way the rules say it is. How do
>you explain to such a person "well, I know the card says that, but we
>changed it because we didn't like it"?

Er, how did the original rule get to be the way it _is_? I thought it
the general can't-use-intercept-unless-you-need-it rule was left out of the
printed rulebooks. If so, just fix this the same way. If not, I would
say there might be argument there for sticking to a rule because it was
printed in the rulebooks. But it seems to me that so much has changed from
the original rulebooks anyway that I hardly think this is a real objection.
The only question is, is the problem bad enough to make one more change?

Fred

We do seem to be at odds over its definition. I wouldn't say I'm the one
who's usage of it is incorrect. Rather than harp about it, though, I'll
try to make myself clear as I go.

>The rule is perfectly clear: "you can't gain intercept unless you need
>it".

The procedure is clearly spelled out. The effect of the rule, however, is
counterintuitive (IMO and by my definition, of course), at least when other
bonuses that might permit a block that would otherwise not be possible.
Hola - we've eliminated almost every card but Second Tradition. Oh, well...

>Now, you may find it counterintuitive (whatever that means);

It means the effect of this rule produces results one wouldn't tend to expect.
In almost every other way (actually, as far as I can think of, _absolutely_
every other way - but then, I haven't considered the issue very rigorously),
stealth is always a good thing for a Vampire to have. When this rule is

any sense.

>why can't Felicia Mostrom see really, _really_ well even if there's no
>stealth, and so on. But if you take no issue with the rule as it
>stands, I don't see how you can take issue with how it applies to 2T.

Who said I "take no issue with the rule as it stands"? In fact, this may
be getting confused by the fact that I _personally_ don't care about the
whole issue that much myself. I can play it perfectly well as it stands.
I just don't quite understand why you take issue with people like Eric who
really don't seem to like it - besides just writing the whole thing off as
a difference in judgement. But it works perfectly well either way. Write
the rule in a way that allows Second Tradition to be used at any time or
keep it as it is. It doesn't really matter.

>Now, if, as Peter has suggested, you want to change the _card_, that's a

If something's got to change, I'd prefer to change the rule. Errata bad.

>
>So, you don't expect it. So what?

So that's bad - or at least, it's a very arguable position that it's bad.
Not treating a game mechanic like stealth in a consistent way could certainly
be seen as a "bad thing" in game design. It depends on what you like.

The above is probably the crux of the whole argument. If you don't accept
it, then you're simple not going to understand the rest of my position.
I'm not sure why you can't see why people might not like an inconsistent
treatment of the concept of stealth in V:tES.

>That doesn't mean the card needs to be changed.

If you think it's bad, it would certainly be a reason.

>Besides which, I think you're misusing the word "reward" here.

"Reward" as in, it's better for an attacker *not* to have stealth than to have
stealth. I think the meaning is quite clear and the usage very appropriate.

>Just because the card works differently than other intercept
>cards doesn't mean it's changing the game dynamic or the general
>inherent value of stealth.

Er, "changing the game dynamic" from what? I didn't say a thing about
"changing the game dynamic". I just said the mechanism of stealth is being
treated inconsistently from (near as I'm aware) every other game situation.

>> To further elaborate, if your game is full of such tricks and traps -

>> the field and make the bad good and stuff like that - then people can plan

its components so that it's a difficult problem to solve. It shouldn't be
very clear whether stealth is worthwhile in general or everyone would either
build all their decks for maximum stealth or for no stealth whatsoever. But
a person may not like *this* particular type of trick, is my point. If they
feel that the value of stealth is perfectly balanced in the game (by how hard
it is to make your Vamps stealthy vs. how much reward you get from stealth)
without slipping in weird situations where you actually don't _want_ to be
stealthy, you wouldn't like the way the rules work now.

>> I just don't think the proposal to change the rules and make it work
>> differently should be villified, either. Debated, certainly. Disputed,
>> perhaps. But not villified.
>
>The thing I don't understand is: why do you think the rules _should_ be
>changed, but the card shouldn't?

Errata bad. Rule changes good. That way - in theory - you can figure out
how to play all cards from just reading a complete set of the rules. Not
having to look up individual cards to see if they're on the "change list".
I suppose either way works reasonably well, in the end. I just prefer less
errata, myself.

>> >> works in (this particular) weird way." It's certainly a reasonable
>> >> opinion.
>
>"I don't like the way this card works so let's change the rules to make
>it work differently"
>
>is very different from
>
>"I don't like the way this card works, so let's discuss how to change it
>to make it work better"

Not really. Changing the rule has the benefits I spoke of above. Plus, if
any other cards fall into this category, you probably won't like how they
currently work for the same reason and you should catch them in the rules
change. Errataing the card means you have to go out and errata any others
that turn up like this. (I'm not sure if there really are any or not. Perhaps
it isn't an issue.)

>> >Because you want the card to work differently. I don't want the card to
>> >work differently. Who wins? I think the best answer is "the rules
>> >win".
>>
>> Er, you mean the _existing_ rules win. Essentially status quo rules uber
>> alle?
>
>I'm not saying that I always agree with the rules. But why should you
>decide which cards should be changed and which not? In light of the DCI
>announcement, that seems to be up to LSJ, not you and not me.

Sure, I agree with that. But this is a different question. First it's
appropriate to discuss changing the rules at all. If the benefits of doing
that are hotly disputed amongst players in the end, perhaps it is better just
to keep things as they are.

>> First of all, explain _why_ some significant number of people are against
>> change.
>
>I will explain why I don't think Second Tradition should be changed:
>
>(1) The way Second Tradition works now is perfectly consistent with the
>simple rule "you can't play intercept unless you need it".
>(2) Second Tradition, as it is, adds an interesting element to the game.
>(3) Second Tradition, as it is, is a perfectly fine card (i.e., it isn't
>wallpaper), nor is it too powerful, so I don't see the need for it to be
>changed.

All right. That's certainly an arguable position. If that's all there is
to it and you can't be convinced otherwise, then there's no point to going
on. Might as well just agree to disagree. Just accept that others don't
necessarily agree that these things are important enough when weighed against
the stealth/consistency problem.

>> the existing rule and just lump it or the rule changes and everybody starts
>> doing it the other way. Either one works.
>
>Except that, AFAIK, the only reason I've seen as to why the rule should
>be changed is "so that Second Tradition will work differently". Why
>should Second Tradition work differently?

See, this the problem I have with your position. You keep questioning it but
when it's explained to you, you simply deny the merits of people wanting to
make stealth a good (or at worst neutral) thing _always_ rather than have it
be a good (or at worst neutral) thing almost all the time except when this
one situation comes up and then it's suddenly a bad thing. Some people don't
like stuff like that. It's not to their taste. And their opinion is as
reasonable and arguable as yours.

Fred

To Frederick Scott and the rest:

I'm not going to try to keep responding point-by-point to every message
on this (now reasonably defunct) subject. I guess what it all boils
down to is that I try to be very conservative when it comes to the issue
of changing cards or rules. Unless there are strong, compelling, and
widely accepted reasons to change the card, I think we're better off
leaving it alone. Why?

Let's take a ficticious card "X". Let's say X is rare, and I've never
owned one. When someone else plays it in a game I'm playing in, how
will I figure out how the card works? I will read it. And through my
thorough knowledge of the game rules (if necessary), I will figure out
what the card does. I will not automatically scan the eratta lists and
clarifications sheets unless I am totally confused about what the card
does, which would rarely happen. I think this is the procedure most
would follow on encountering a new or obscure card. The more rules
changes and card eratta there is, the less likely this is to work, and
hence the more complex the game becomes. [Note: often complexity is
good in a game, but this is the bad kind of complexity. Kind of like
the combat dice rolling in Age of Rennaisance, for example]

Sometimes card eratta is necessary. In the case where the card text
contradicts common sense (it's a reaction card that says "+1 stealth",
for example), contradicts the rules in a way that is perceived to be bad
for the game, or the card is otherwise unusable as is. When there is
nothing inherently wrong with the card (ex.: Second Tradition, Immortal
Grapple [RRRRR...], and so on), why complicate matters by changing the
cards? Granted, if playtesting and/or design had gone more smoothly,
this wouldn't be as much of an issue, but alas, here we are.

To me, personal distaste with a card or its effects is not sufficient
grounds to go throwing a monkey wrench into the works.

Here's another example: Thoughts Betrayed. Lots of people really don't
like this card. But if you go back (via DejaNews, I guess) to the
discussions on this card right after its release, the most cogent
arguments to change the card were not "I hate this card, let's change
it". They were "here's how the card breaks the game" or "here's how the
card is counter to everything that is Jyhad" or simply "here's how the
card is too powerful". Second Tradition does not do any of these
things.

Re: "counterintuitive" vs. "unexpected". I wasn't trying to be snippy.
I simply tried to comment that "unexpected" is hardly ever a bad thing,
while "counterintuitive" might be, if we could figure out what you mean
when you use that word. And please, don't hash through this again.

I support card changes if I feel they are beneficial to the game as a
whole, but I am reluctant to if the only effect they would have is to
change some people's perceptions of the game.

And finally, I will never begrudge anyone the right to discuss anything.
Heck, I've still got a bone or two to pick with LSJ over that supremely
wack Immortal Grapple ruling. Actually, I've got a whole graveyard of
bones to pick. I am not arguing against arguing. And if I attempt to
reason logically, chalk that up to my being a Math PhD student. It's
just the way I am.

See, I can be civil, too! :)
